scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Yablochko emerged as an urban Russian dance in the 1910s, combining the British and Irish hornpipe with traditional Russian dances like the Barynya.
The hornpipe had entered Russian naval circles in the late nineteenth century and was popularized on café-concert stages as the 'matelot'.

During the Russian Civil War (1917–1921), the dance merged with topical chastushka verses sung by Red, White, Green, and Black forces, transforming it into an iconic symbol of the revolutionary sailor.
on_screen: Map: Russia · Europe
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Originally an outlet for revolutionary sailors and wartime soldiers, the dance accompanied biting political chastushkas during the Russian Civil War.
During the Great Patriotic War, military units formed cultural brigades featuring their own versions of the dance to sustain morale.
It functions as a celebratory demonstration of agility, humor, and collective naval identity.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage: Igor Moiseyev Ballet - Yablochko (1982) (https://archive.org/details/igor-moiseyev-ballet-yablochko-1982)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is arranged in phrases of 8 to 16 bars over a musical square, beginning slowly and accelerating to a very fast tempo.
Performers begin with a slow entrance and broad hand gestures, line up with hands on one another's shoulders, and execute rapid foot-tapping and stomping.
Watch for Prisiadka, Chechotka, Khlopushka.

Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Linear chorus lines, stationary fixed-spot center stage, and circular call-and-response spaces

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The dance tune is played in a minor key at tempos ranging from slow to very fast.
It is played on the garmoshka (Russian button accordion) or folk and symphonic orchestra instruments.
Listen for the Garmoshka, Symphony orchestra, Folk orchestra.
The pulse is 2/4.

A punchy, minor-key chastushka melody driven by rhythmic button accordion or brass-heavy orchestral syncopation. Phrases cycle in rigid 8-to-16-measure squares that begin at a stately, swaggering tempo before steadily accelerating into a breakneck percussive sprint.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Yablochko is performed by dancers wearing naval sailor uniforms, complete with sailor caps referencing the naval pompom.

Originally performed on ship decks, military grounds, and street corners, it transitioned into concert halls and theaters, famously featured on the Bolshoi Theatre stage and in the touring repertoire of the Moiseyev Ballet.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Reinhold Glière incorporated the choreography into his 1926 ballet The Red Poppy at the Bolshoi Theatre.
Singer David Medoff produced one of the earliest known audio recordings for Columbia Records in New York in 1923.
Variants developed within different military fleets and armies, notably the Black Sea Fleet where Ukrainian sailor songs influenced the melody.
Yablochko descends from the British and Irish hornpipe synthesized with the Russian Barynya folk dance and café-concert matelot performances.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Yablochko is parent of Hornpipe: British and Irish hornpipe dances brought by sailors served as a primary structural ancestor to Yablochko.
Yablochko is parent of Barynya: Traditional Russian folk dance whose energetic steps and squat motifs synthesized with the hornpipe.
Yablochko is sibling of Tsyganochka: Shares the uncommon feature of being a Russian folk dance performed in a minor key.
